awd_titl_txt: POSE: Phase I: Planning an Open-Source Ecosystem Approach for the ZMap Toolkit
awd_abstract_narration:
This Pathways to Enable Open-Source Ecosystems (POSE) project provides cybersecurity and networking researchers, in academia, government, and industry, a reliable open-source software toolkit for measuring and monitoring Internet infrastructure at a global scale. Real-time, global visibility into Internet infrastructure (e.g., servers, websites, critical infrastructure, and other Internet-connected devices that compose the Internet) is paramount for uncovering security weaknesses, for fixing vulnerabilities before they can be attacked, and for guiding the deployment of more performant and secure Internet protocols. This project builds the foundation to transform a frequently utilized Internet measurement toolkit for finding, understanding, and securing tens of millions of Internet devices and the most depended on protocols into a self-sustaining open-source community that can operate without government funding long-term. This community will maintain and improve this toolkit, as well as help education and support new users, such that it can continue to serve as the technical foundation for academic research and industry solutions that protect the core of the Internet and the infrastructure connected to it.

This POSE project enables ecosystem discovery with the communities (e.g., academic researchers, Internet security companies, certificate authorities) that use the ZMap Internet Measurement Toolkit (e.g., ZMap, ZGrab, ZDNS, ZLint tools) to understand their needs, frustrations, use, appetite for providing financial or in-kind support, and their requirements for long-term support. The project will also enable an understanding of how best to build community, support, and documentation around the toolkit that enables further deployment and utilization of data to improve Internet security. This project will develop a plan to transform the ZMap Toolkit from an open-source toolkit into a healthy, self-sustaining open-source ecosystem.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The open source ZMap Internet Measurement toolkit (i.e., ZMap, ZGrab, ZDNS, and other associated tools) enables large-scale, global measurement of Internet hosts, services, names, and certificates. It has been the foundation of more than 300 peer-reviewed networking, security, and Internet research papers and has been used across the cybersecurity industry to protect the Internet perimeters of organizations.

The resulting research has uncovered protocol weaknesses in TLS and SSH, guided the strengthening of the most commonly deployed cryptographic primitives (e.g., Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange), improved the WebPKI, enabled widespread vulnerability notifications, and shed light on security weaknesses in IoT devices, industrial control systems, and security-critical Internet infrastructure.

Yet, despite its widespread usage, ZMap has seen relatively little community contribution to the code base beyond a small set of core contributors. In this project, the research team interviewed 100 community members, including 51 academic researchers, 11 open source contributors, 10 certificate authorities, 8 attack surface management companies, and 4 web browsers to better understand their needs, limitations of ZMap for their use cases, and what would be needed for them to more actively participate in the open source ecosystem.

The team identified several themes in what prevented more in-depth participation from groups, including: (1) lack of documentation about how to use tools; (2) a catch-22 where the lack of timely review on contributions precluded contribution but also the type of participation needed to review contributions; (3) unclear bar and expectations for contribution as well as best practcies as to how to best contribute; and (4) lack of domain expertise from some of the most resourced users.

Beyond interviews, we collected feedback from participants on different structures for providing project support, acceptable project governance rules, and how best to build a community across both academic research and industry.

In response to feedback, the team: (1) developed cross-tool tutorials and documentation beyond the specifics of how to use tools to help new users, (2) improved CI/CD pipelines to help test new pull requests, (3) added additional testing to improve ability to merge in contributions, (4) marked issues that would be a good starting point for new contributors, and (5) added both contribution guidelines and issue templates to support future contributions.

Last, we addressed long-standing pull requests and issues across projects, such that projects are in clean health for new developers to contribute to them, merging a total 340 pull requests across ZMap, ZGrab, ZDNS, and ZCrypto.
